caption: I've mixed hair bleach for thirty-four years and I wear gloves to handle persulfate. Then a client in my chair asked what I soak my partial in, and I finally read the box.
headline: I wear gloves for this chemical. It was in my mouth.
alt_hooks:
Every morning I put on gloves to mix bleach powder.

Every night I soaked my teeth in the same chemical.

It took a client in my chair to point it out.

My upper lip was swollen for three months, and my dentist had no idea why.

A dental hygienist figured it out in my salon chair, halfway through her root touch-up.
script:
I've mixed hair bleach for thirty-four years. I know exactly what persulfate does to skin.

So picture my face when I found that same word on the box I soaked my teeth in. Every single night.

My lip had been swollen for three months. My dentist couldn't tell me why. A client figured it out from my salon chair, and I'll tell you what she said.

Let me back up.

I'm Roz. I'm fifty-eight. I own a four-chair salon in Fargo, North Dakota. Color is my thing.

Six years ago I lost four upper teeth to a fall on the ice. I've worn a partial ever since.

I cleaned it the way I was told. Brush in the morning. One Polident tablet in a glass every night. Eight dollars a box, forever.

Persulfate is the booster in bleach powder. It's what makes lightener lift.

It's also why stylists get cracked hands. Some quit because their lungs tighten up over the mixing bowl.

I wear gloves and a mask for it. Then I went home and put it in my mouth.

Here's what last winter took from me. Remember these.

My lip. Puffy and tight every morning. Red lipstick is my signature. I stopped wearing it. It just made people stare.

My gums. A burning line right where the partial sits. Like a sunburn that never peeled.

And my chair. I lean in close to talk to clients. I stopped leaning. I talked to them through the mirror.

My dentist blamed the adhesive. I switched. I scrubbed harder. I bought extra-strength tablets. I tried a twenty-nine dollar ultrasonic thing off Amazon that hummed and did nothing.

It got worse.

In February, Monique sat in my chair. Dental hygienist, twenty years.

She watched me in the mirror. "Roz, what do you soak that partial in?"

I told her.

She put down her magazine. "That's persulfate, Roz. Same stuff that's in your lightener."

Thirty-four years with that chemical, and I'd never once read the box.

She told me the FDA warned about allergic reactions to persulfate in denture cleansers back in 2008. Swelling. Hives. Burning gums. Trouble breathing. At least one death.

Then she said something worse.

"And it isn't even cleaning it."

A tablet works on the surface. But acrylic is full of tiny pores and scratches. Germs live down in there as a slime called biofilm. The fizz never reaches it.

And scrubbing harder just makes more scratches to move into.

She put it in my language. "It's dry shampoo, Roz. Smells great. Looks clean. The scalp underneath is still dirty."

Her test: after the soak, run your fingernail along the inside of the plate.

Slick. Almost slippery. After eight hours in chemicals.

Try yours tonight. If it feels like that, it's biofilm. Minty, and alive.

Monique said a real clean needs four things.

It has to get into the pores, not just the surface.

It has to kill what it shakes loose.

No chemicals.

And quick enough to do every day.

She uses the DentalPULSE Pod on her own night guard.

Forty-two thousand ultrasonic vibrations a second reach into every scratch. Then medical-grade UV-C light. Tap water. Five minutes.

In a ninety-day lab test of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners, six of seven left live bacteria. This one came out on top.

I filled it at my shampoo bowl, dropped the partial in, and pressed the button.

Five minutes later the water was cloudy. Then brown.

Six years of nightly chemicals, and that's what was left.

My lip went down in two weeks. I wear red again.

By week three, the burning line on my gums was gone.

And I lean in. Right beside them, the way I always did.

That last box of tablets sits in my back room now, next to the lightener. Where persulfate belongs.

A tablet only touches the surface, and you soak it all night in something I wear gloves to handle.

headline: What I found under my mother's sink
alt_hooks:
Twenty-two years.

Every night, my mother soaked her teeth in a glass of blue water.

Then one Tuesday she opened the door with a towel over her mouth.

The nurse looked at my mom's swollen lip.

Then at the box in my hand.

"How long has she been using these?"
script:
My mother's top lip was twice its normal size.

She said it was a cold sore.

It wasn't a cold sore.

The answer was under her bathroom sink. In a box she'd been buying for twenty-two years.

And wait till you hear what she said when she saw the water.

Let me back up.

I'm Tess. I'm forty-four. I deliver mail in Tacoma, Washington.

My mom, Carol, is seventy-seven. Full upper and lower since her fifties.

I eat lunch at her kitchen table every Tuesday.

That Tuesday in August, she opened the door with a dish towel pressed to her mouth.

Her lip was swollen tight and shiny. Her gums were angry red.

"It's nothing, Tessie. Allergies."

My mother has never had an allergy in her life.

Here's what that summer had already cost her.

Remember these.

Choir. Forty years in the alto section at St. Anne's. She quit in June.

Apples. She ate one every afternoon of my childhood. Then she stopped buying them.

And the grandkids' video calls. She started pointing the camera at the ceiling.

I went for an ice pack. The cabinet under her sink was open.

Polident. Three boxes.

And a glass on the counter, still cloudy blue from last night.

She'd been soaking her teeth in it overnight. Every night.

Two tablets lately, she said. "To get them extra clean."

I turned the box over.

Persulfate.

And a warning in tiny print about allergic reactions.

I took her to urgent care that afternoon.

The nurse practitioner looked at her lip. Then at the box in my hand.

"How long has she used these?"

"Twenty-two years."

The FDA warned about this back in 2008.

Allergic reactions to persulfate in denture cleansers. Swollen lips. Burning gums. Hives. Trouble breathing.

At least one death.

Then she said the worst part.

"Honestly? It isn't even getting them clean."

A tablet works on the surface.

Dentures are acrylic, full of tiny pores and scratches.

Germs live down in there as a film. Biofilm.

The fizz doesn't reach it.

Scrubbing harder just carves more hiding places.

"It's like bleaching moldy grout," she said. "White on top. The mold is still in the grout."

Every night, a chemical bath that couldn't reach the germs. Every morning, both back in her mouth.

That night I tried her test.

After the soak, wipe a white paper towel along the inside of the plate.

A yellow-gray smear.

After eight hours in chemicals.

Try it tonight. It's free.

We switched to dish soap and a brush. The swelling went down. But the film and the smell came back.

I bought a twenty-nine dollar ultrasonic thing online. It buzzed. Nothing changed.

The nurse had given me a list.

It has to do four things.

One. Reach into the pores, not just the surface.

Two. Kill what it shakes loose.

Three. No chemicals. None.

Four. Quick enough to do every day.

Only one thing checked all four.

The DentalPULSE Pod.

Forty-two thousand ultrasonic vibrations a second, into every scratch.

Then medical-grade UV-C light.

Tap water. Five minutes. One button.

In a ninety-day lab test, six of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners left live bacteria.

This was the one that didn't.

The next Tuesday I brought it to lunch.

Mom dropped her teeth in and pressed the button.

We stood there and watched.

Cloudy.

Then brown.

Mom put her hand over her mouth.

"Tessie. That was in my mouth."

That was four months ago.

Her gums are pink. The swelling never came back.

She rejoined the altos. She sang at Christmas Eve mass. I cried in the back pew.

Last week she bit straight into a Honeycrisp, laughing.

And the camera points at her face again. The grandkids say Grandma talks too much now.

Last Tuesday I opened the cabinet under her sink.

caption: I added up twenty years of denture tablets: seven thousand three hundred of them. My son-in-law glanced at the total and found a much scarier number in it.
headline: I added up 20 years of denture tablets
alt_hooks:
Fourteen hundred and sixty dollars.

That's what I spent soaking my teeth in a glass for twenty years.

And that's the least of what it cost me.

My grandson climbed in my lap and said, "Grandpa, your mouth smells like the pond."

I'd used a denture tablet every single night for twenty years.
script:
Seven thousand three hundred.

That's how many denture tablets I've dropped in a glass. I'm a bookkeeper. I kept the receipts.

The money wasn't the number that scared me. My son-in-law found that one.

And it took my wife three words to tell me I'd finally fixed it.

Let me back up.

I'm Len. I'm sixty-six. I kept the books for a grain co-op in Salina, Kansas, for thirty-one years.

Full dentures at forty-six. Every night since: brush them, drop a Polident in the glass, soak till morning.

Last April, doing taxes at the kitchen table, I pulled every pharmacy receipt in the shoebox and ran a tape.

Seven thousand three hundred tablets. About twenty cents apiece. Fourteen hundred and sixty dollars.

Plus a twenty-nine dollar ultrasonic gadget that buzzed for a month and quit.

But here's what I didn't have a column for.

My wife, Nadine, stopped kissing me good morning. Just my cheek now. She never said why.

My grandson Caleb is nine. He climbed in my lap in March and said, "Grandpa, your mouth smells like the pond."

And Friday nights I called Legion bingo. Microphone right at my mouth. I quit. I could smell myself through that thing.

In May, my son-in-law Dev came for Sunday dinner. He cleans surgical instruments at the hospital.

I showed him my tape. He didn't look at the dollars. He looked at the count.

"Len. That's seven thousand three hundred overnight chemical baths. For something that goes in your mouth."

What was in them? Twenty years, and I'd never read the box.

Persulfate.

Dev told me the FDA warned about allergic reactions to persulfate in denture cleansers back in 2008. Burning gums. Swelling. Hives. Breathing problems. At least one death.

I'd had a raw, sore roof of the mouth for two years. I blamed the fit.

Then Dev said, "And it isn't even cleaning them."

At the hospital, he said, nobody soaks an instrument and calls it clean. A soak only loosens the top layer.

Dentures are acrylic, full of tiny pores and scratches. Germs live down in there as a slime called biofilm. The fizz never gets in. And brushing carves new scratches for them.

"You know that casserole dish you soak overnight?" he said. "The loose stuff floats off. The baked-on corners are still there in the morning."

His test: after tonight's soak, drop your denture in a sandwich bag. Seal it. Wait an hour. Open it and smell.

I did. I had to sit down. That smell was coming out of the pores, after eight hours in chemicals.

Dev listed four things a real clean needs.

One. It has to get into the pores, not just the surface.

Two. It has to kill what it shakes loose.

Three. No chemicals. Nothing to buy every month.

Four. Quick enough to do every day.

"That's how we do instruments," he said. "Ultrasonic first. Then you kill what's left."

He'd already found one. The DentalPULSE Pod.

Forty-two thousand ultrasonic vibrations a second, into every scratch. Then medical-grade UV-C light. Tap water. Five minutes.

In a ninety-day lab test of seven leading ultrasonic cleaners, six of seven left live bacteria. This one came out on top.

First cycle, Nadine watched.

Cloudy at two minutes. Brown at five.

Twenty years of tablets, and that's what they'd been sleeping in.

The bag test the next morning? Just plastic.

The roof of my mouth stopped burning in about three weeks.

On the Fourth of July, Caleb climbed in my lap and never mentioned the pond. Just his lizard.

I'm back calling bingo. Mouth right on the microphone.

And last Tuesday Nadine kissed me good morning. On the mouth. "There you are," she said.

There's still a column in my ledger marked tablets.

This month I wrote a zero in it. Best number I've ever posted.
